paragraphs.heading: A rock that splits into sheets
paragraphs.text: Slate is a fine-grained metamorphic rock. It shows no obvious layers of differing composition, yet it splits easily into thin slabs and plates. It usually forms when mudrock goes through low-grade regional metamorphism.

paragraphs.heading: Where the splitting planes come from
paragraphs.text: The planes slate splits along are called slaty cleavage. Strong compression causes them: fine-grained clay regrows as flakes in planes at right angles to the squeeze. These planes may not match the layers of the original sediment. Their direction is independent of any sedimentary structures in the mudrock and reflects the direction of regional compression.

paragraphs.heading: From mudrock to slate
paragraphs.text: As mudrock is compacted into slate it loses up to 50% of its volume. Grains of platy minerals, such as clay minerals, are turned into parallel layers at right angles to the direction of compaction, and these start to give the rock its cleavage. Once the clay minerals start changing into chlorite and mica, the cleavage is fully developed. Organic carbon in the rock becomes graphite.

paragraphs.heading: Up close
paragraphs.text: The metamorphism is mild, so the mineral crystals stay microscopic and a freshly split surface looks dull. Phyllite, the next-higher grade of metamorphic rock that comes from mudstone, has silky split surfaces instead. The cleavage planes in slate sit too close together to be made out in a hand sample. Under a microscope, slate turns out to be very thin lenses of quartz and feldspar separated by layers of mica, typically less than 100 μm thick.

paragraphs.heading: What survives inside
paragraphs.text: Slate formed in low heat and pressure compared with most other metamorphic rocks. For that reason some fossils can be found in it. Sometimes even the microscopic remains of delicate organisms turn up.

paragraphs.heading: Why it ends up on roofs
paragraphs.text: Many slates, struck parallel to the foliation with a special tool in the quarry, come apart as smooth, flat sheets. This property is called fissility, and such sheets have a long history of use in roofs, floor tiles and billiard tables. Slate has an extremely low water absorption index, under 0.4%, which makes it resistant to frost damage. Slate can last for several hundred years, and often needs little or no maintenance.

paragraphs.heading: The slate you write on
paragraphs.text: By tradition, a writing slate was a small piece of the rock, smooth and often set in a wooden frame. People wrote on it with chalk and used it as a notepad or notice board, especially to record charges in pubs and inns. This is where the phrases "blank slate" and "clean slate" come from.
